justification: This is round 2's independent read, then checked against round 1. The article remains clearly ahead of what actually ranks for this query: every comparison page checked (this round and round 1's) is a feature list or a doubling explainer with no measurements and no primary sources, while this article backs every mechanism with a program a reader can run and a source it was checked against (10 sources now 12, each cited at the point of the claim; List.cs claims for the uint bounds-check cast, _version, RemoveAll's two-index pass and GrowForInsertion all match the real source). It also corrects a claim the competing pages state without evidence -- that arrays read faster than List<T> -- with its own measurement showing the three contiguous containers within run-to-run noise of each other. Round 1's major finding was that the 'measure one cache line' exercise reproduced the first example of Igor Ostrovsky's Gallery of Processor Cache Effects (varying stride 1-16 over a large array, same conclusion) without credit. I re-fetched Ostrovsky's page and re-read all seven of its examples against the current article: that exercise is gone. In its place, the column-first section now runs its own tiled/banded experiment that tests two hypotheses the article itself raised (reuse distance, and a power-of-two stride hitting cache associativity at n=4096) by padding the row and by summing in bands of 16 -- a different measurement, on different data, built to falsify or confirm this article's own claims rather than reproduce Ostrovsky's stride-sweep. The jagged-array banding exercise later in the piece (testing whether re-reading g[r] explains its column-first slowness) has no counterpart on Ostrovsky's page at all. Both are genuinely this article's own constructions, not reworded copies -- the fix is real, not cosmetic. Of round 1's five minor issues, four are verifiably fixed: the 0-based-indexing sentence is now scoped to the arithmetic ('keeps the formula simplest') rather than claimed as history; the 'flat' claim about row-first cost now says '0.7 to 0.9 ns from 500 upward' and explains the small-grid exception, which matches the table; the five count-announcing lead-ins ('Three things...', 'Each line has something to say...') are gone; and the closing section no longer restates the thesis, while the pre-sizing bullet is now scoped ('skips the regrowth copy' only 'up to n', not 'every regrowth copy'). One minor is not fixed (see issues). Five distinctive sentences were spot-checked this round by web search in quotation marks and none returned a match, consistent with round 1's finding of no copied text. Structure still does not template against the two other published articles opened for comparison (big-o-notation.md, amortized-analysis.md): heading sets, exercise framing and openings all differ. What keeps this below the top of the scale: the one unfixed minor, a still-long article whose value is earned but whose density asks a lot of a first-time reader, and the fact that a couple of the causal explanations (the 4096 anomaly, the jagged reference-read cost) remain hedged hypotheses rather than confirmed measurements -- appropriately hedged, but not a fully closed case the way MDN-grade reference material would leave it.
